content: Health providers also face challenges, such as high workloads and insufficient training in communicating with newly diagnosed TB patients, which hinder effective screening. To implement a community-based model for child contact investigations, several prerequisites were identified. These include training community health workers (CHWs) in conducting and motivating contact investigations, using checklists for symptoms and adherence to TB preventive therapy (TPT), providing secure transportation for CHWs, dispensing medications at health facilities, utilizing TPT cards, and ensuring effective communication between TB focal persons, CHWs, and index TB cases. Strengths of the community-based model include the flexibility to organize household visits, the ability to screen entire households simultaneously, addressing other health issues during TB investigations, integrating care for both contacts and index cases, and saving time and financial resources for households. However, challenges include reluctance of index patients to disclose their TB status, the need for additional human and financial resources, and the importance of establishing robust monitoring and reporting systems. Screening for TB in children and adolescents aims to identify those with presumptive TB who require further evaluation to confirm the diagnosis. It also identifies individuals eligible for and likely to benefit from TPT. Screening tests are not diagnostic; individuals with positive results must undergo further evaluation. Children and adolescents living with HIV should be systematically screened for TB at every health facility visit. Household contacts of TB patients should also be screened during contact investigations or follow-up of the index patient’s treatment. For children under 15 years who are close contacts of TB patients, systematic screening should involve symptom screening (e.g., cough lasting more than two weeks, fever for more than two weeks, or poor weight gain in the past three months) and/or chest X-rays (CXR). Symptoms of TB in children are often nonspecific and overlap with other childhood illnesses, leading to delayed diagnosis. Certain forms of TB, such as central nervous system TB, carry a high risk of death or permanent disability if detected late, even with treatment. Medical emergencies like TB meningitis, disseminated TB, and spinal TB require immediate recognition and referral to appropriate care. The Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine reduces the risk of severe TB forms, such as TB meningitis and miliary TB, but its protection is incomplete. Screening considerations apply regardless of BCG immunization status. Children living with HIV are at significantly higher risk of rapid progression to severe TB disease and death if undiagnosed. They should be screened for TB at every healthcare encounter, as they are five times more likely to develop TB than HIV-negative children. Even with antiretroviral therapy (ART), their risk remains elevated. Symptom screening for TB in children under 10 years who are close contacts of TB patients should include cough, fever, and poor weight gain. In young children, reduced playfulness or lethargy may also indicate TB, as prolonged cough may be absent in disseminated disease. Growth charts should be reviewed regularly to identify weight loss or failure to thrive, which are warning signs of possible TB. Chest X-rays are more specific than symptom screening alone for detecting TB in children. However, abnormalities caused by TB in children may differ from those in adults, and findings can be subtle, especially in younger children. Both posteroanterior and lateral views are recommended for optimal evaluation. Mobile CXR units can improve access in underserved areas but require logistical and financial support. Digital X-ray machines emit minimal radiation, posing very low risk to patients. Molecular diagnostic tests, such as WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs), are not currently recommended for TB screening in children but should be used to confirm TB in those who screen positive. Tests for TB infection, such as the tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), should not be used for TB disease screening in children, as they cannot distinguish between TB infection and active disease. Contact investigations should screen close contacts of TB patients for symptoms and/or CXR abnormalities, followed by appropriate diagnostic evaluation. However, contact investigations can be resource-intensive and may risk stigma for households. Health workers can encourage TB patients to bring their contacts, including children, to health facilities for screening. Barriers such as financial constraints, time limitations, and distrust of healthcare services should be addressed when designing local approaches. Children exposed to TB but found not to have active disease should be assessed for TB infection and eligibility for TPT. Asymptomatic close contacts aged five years and older should undergo CXR if available, and further evaluation if abnormalities are detected. CXR is not required before starting TPT in asymptomatic close contacts under five years old if TB disease is ruled out through symptom screening. Children living with HIV should be closely monitored within the healthcare system and screened for TB at every encounter, including routine visits such as vaccination days or nutritional support programs. Despite the low specificity of symptom screening, the benefits of TB treatment outweigh the risks of over-investigation and treatment, given the high mortality associated with untreated TB in this population. BCG vaccination is recommended for all healthy neonates in high TB incidence settings. However, children living with HIV should not receive BCG due to the risk of disseminated BCG disease unless they are on ART, clinically well, and immunologically stable. Neonates born to mothers with confirmed TB should receive TPT after ruling out active disease and be monitored for TB symptoms. If asymptomatic and HIV-negative, they should receive BCG vaccination two weeks after completing TPT. In summary, systematic TB screening and prevention strategies, including BCG vaccination and TPT, are critical for reducing TB-related morbidity and mortality in children and adolescents, particularly those living with HIV or in close contact with TB patients.
